label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
read: RC2 70-page edition, draft: manuscript/rc2/70/ (17 files, the storyteller's new order) and its 61-page PDF built at 521f9e72
where_i_skimmed_or_stopped: 04: a long run of role introductions; I wanted to build one agent, not meet nine
05: the walked-through wake record is clear, but 'pre-review', 'post-check' and 'finding' pile up
08: the register counts (210, 55, 52) and the release-history row feel like someone else's job
11: the three answers about why the hold was called, and the lost-correction story, are inside baseball
14: the nine-then-eight cast list and the 'third factory, planned' section, which is a plan not a result
first_thing_i_would_do: Write the one page of rules for a single agent (what it is for, what it may change, when it stops and asks me) from the start-here page, using the shop owner's example as a template.
price: about 8 to 10 pounds as an ebook; I would not pay more for a paperback that is mostly a day's diary
why: The start-here page and chapter 16 are exactly the next step after my first build, and the 'do this now' boxes make it feel doable. But I had to wade through a lot of timestamps, commit hashes and agent names before getting to anything I could use, and it sometimes read as if for programmers (repository, commit, scope, scope check, git). A shorter 'method first, story second' book I would buy at once.

by_chapter.why: Warm, clear and about me: slides cannot move, so you talk over them. The loop (see, ask, see again) is the first idea I could use.
by_chapter.quote: I was the bit in between.

by_chapter.why: The best page in the book for me: five ticks, no jargon beyond 'agent'. I would have liked it first, and the box for printing is still a 'Figure to come'.
by_chapter.quote: If you want to start now, this page is all you need.

by_chapter.why: A tour of what got made reassures me it is real. Page counts (58 beats, 162 wakes, 439 commits) bounce around a bit, and the 163 versus 162 aside is a detour I do not need.
Rules page, brief, reality file, check and hold in one chapter: this is the core, and the shop owner's example is what I would copy. The quoted CLAUDE.md lines are a bit technical.
by_chapter.quote: A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says.

by_chapter.why: Nine characters introduced in one go with similar voices. 'Scope', 'policy' and 'empty chair' arrive quickly. The one line I kept was the scope-is-a-setting idea.
by_chapter.quote: A scope is a setting, not a boundary: it catches mistakes, not a steered agent.

by_chapter.why: The five-step wake is the hardest idea and is explained by a technical case (a wake record with 'partial' and 'finding'). I understood the shape after the picture on page 24, not the text. 'Not a second identity' is memorable but abstract.
by_chapter.quote: a second reading, not a second identity.

by_chapter.why: Letters as files in folders is easy to picture and I could do it tomorrow. The commit notes ('To-ruv-sgit') are too git-specific for me.
The trigger chart is a good picture but the chapter is a diary of nine hours. The 'if it is not in a file, it did not happen' line is the take-away.
by_chapter.quote: If it is not in a file, it did not happen.

by_chapter.why: Four pipes is a useful frame, then register counts and release history lose me. The unused corrections file is a good honest point.
by_chapter.quote: A brief that is never corrected becomes a story about what you thought you wanted.

by_chapter.why: Loop and port: 'port, not rebuild' is useful, the rest is a timeline of asks and agents I have not memorised.
Tension and a clear story: the hold file in one minute. 'No member lifts it' is a rule I would copy today.
by_chapter.quote: I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.

by_chapter.why: I like that failures stay in, but five misses told with timestamps and a missing lock tool is hard to relate to. The freeze-and-write-down-what-waits lesson is good.
by_chapter.quote: when you freeze something, write down what is waiting to go in when you unfreeze it.

by_chapter.why: Insider, reach, second reading: the argument is serious but for security people; I lost the thread of why it matters to my small project until the last section.
A session is not a member is a valuable idea for me (the agent forgets), but the handover tour is heavy.
by_chapter.quote: only what it wrote down survives.

by_chapter.why: The cast list of eight more agents scared me off; 'you need three' rescued it. The planned third factory is thin.
by_chapter.quote: A first team needs three: one that keeps the time and the plan, one that builds, and one that checks every fact and number.

by_chapter.why: Where I would start. Five steps with examples I can copy and the checklist. Too late in the book, and a few lines point back to 'part 3, chapter 8' which means flipping.
by_chapter.quote: Ship something somebody else can use, then do it again.

by_chapter.why: Handy, and it is where I would have liked to start with an unknown word. Missing 'gate', 'port' and 'policy' as entries.

pages_too_tight: p5 to p6: a quote block, a screenshot and several quoted passages with small caption text
p16 and p24: tiny wake-record text and captions I could barely read on a phone
p31 and p34: figure captions with source ids (C071, C023) in very small type
p29: two commit cards with tiny type
p59: the checklist is dense, small italic text
best_line: Ship something somebody else can use, then do it again.
worst_moment: Chapter 5, the wake record: 'Step four, the post-review... agents.py flags CLAUDE.md as outside conductor scope' style detail; I felt this was for programmers.
top_three_changes: Put the start-here page and a shortened chapter 16 up front, and draw the printable sheet; then tell the story as the reason it works.
Cut or compress chapters 4, 8, 9 and 12, which are the diary and the security argument, and keep only the lines I would copy.
Explain git words (repository, commit, scope, policy, port) in plain language where first used, and cut hashes, ids and timestamps from the main text.
notes: The voice is warm and honest and I trust the author because failures are shown. The risk is that a reader like me thinks it is a book for people who already run teams of agents, until chapter 16. Many figure captions repeat the text. Dramatised scenes with agent personalities are charming and help me follow, but the 'Where this came from' sections are for the team, not me.
